amount of air swallowed increases with eating or drinking 
too fast, smoking, chewing gum, sucking on hard candy, us-
ing a straw, drinking carbonated drinks, and wearing loose-
fitting dentures. Foods that produce gas in one person may 
not cause gas in someone else, depending on the mix of mi-
croorganisms in the individual’s colon. Inactivity, decreased 
motility, aerophagia, dietary components, and certain GI 
disorders can alter the amount of intestinal gas and individ-
ual symptoms.
Normally, the concentration of bacteria in the small intes-
tine is significantly lower than that found in the colon. Various 
conditions can lead to overgrowth of bacteria in the small intes-
tine causing bloating, distention, nausea, diarrhea, or other
